money_at_stake.rationale: Re-verification pass, 2026-08-30: three of the five originally cited items did not hold up on fetch and are deleted rather than repaired. (1) The Solar Power World citation, used for a claimed USD ~14 billion Jan-Oct 2024 import figure, contains no dollar figures anywhere in the article, only GW volumes (it does correctly discuss 54.3 GW of finished panels and 13.89 GW of silicon cells for 2024, but that is a different fact than the one the claim rested on). (2) The pv-magazine-usa.com 86 GW / 43.4 GW article returned HTTP 403 Forbidden on two direct fetch attempts and could not be reached via the Wayback Machine either (this tool cannot fetch web.archive.org at all), so it is unverifiable rather than merely unopened. (3) The Sunhub cost-per-watt citation states materially different figures than the claim asserted (the page says USD 0.90-1.30/W utility-scale and USD 1.40-2.20/W commercial, not USD 1.06-1.20 and USD 1.44-1.72) and carries a different publication date (2026-06-04 on the page, not 2026-01-28 as originally cited), a pattern consistent with the source never having been opened. What survives, fetched and quoted this run: GTAIC's trailing-12-month (Aug 2024 to Jul 2025) US solar module import value of USD 8.40 billion, and Troutman Pepper Locke's confirmation that the Section 232 minimum-import-price regime covers the full downstream chain (polysilicon, ingots and wafers, cells, and modules), not modules alone. USD 8.40 billion on its own sits below the USD 10 billion line, and while the Troutman citation supports that the true covered-chain trade value runs larger than the module-only figure, no surviving cited source quantifies the additional polysilicon, ingot/wafer, or cell trade value, so there is no cited basis left to place the total above USD 10 billion. Banded on the one hard cited figure that survived verification: B1_10, down from the prior appraisal's B10_100, because the corroborating figures that had carried it there did not survive a fetch.

evidence.source_excerpt: The minimum import price program sets price floors of $21/kg for polysilicon, $100/kg for ingots and wafers, $0.22/W for solar cells, and $0.38/W for solar modules... a flat 15% ad valorem tariff on downstream derivatives.

public_reach.rationale: Re-verification pass, 2026-08-30: two of the three originally cited items did not hold up on fetch. The Troutman Pepper Locke article, cited for REC Silicon's exit from the polysilicon market and for Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker Chemie being the two remaining producers, contains none of those three names anywhere in its text; it states only a different, more general fact (US polysilicon production fell from roughly 50% of global share in 2005 to under 2% in 2024). The PV Tech Hemlock article, cited for Hemlock being the sole US-owned hyper-pure polysilicon manufacturer and a private joint venture of Corning, Shin-Etsu and Mitsubishi Materials, supports only the USD 325 million CHIPS Act funding figure; it says nothing about ownership structure or joint-venture status. Both are deleted rather than repaired. What survives is the PV Tech concentration article: Chinese firms hold nine of the top ten global polysilicon producer positions, with the top four (Tongwei, GCL Technology, Daqo New Energy, Xinte Energy) holding 65% of 2024 output, and Wacker Chemie, a diversified German chemicals company for whom polysilicon is one segment rather than a pure play, the sole non-Chinese firm in the top ten. That is a strong, cited case that the mechanism's own named commodity, polysilicon, is majority produced by firms not reasonably reachable from a Western brokerage account. The downstream counter-argument this appraisal previously made, that the utility-scale developers and non-Chinese cell/module assemblers riding this build-out are broadly listed, is retained as judgment rather than deleted outright, because it is a reasonable industry-structure inference, but it now rests on no surviving cited source at the level of a specific company census, since the two items that had been doing that work are gone. Scored below the prior appraisal's midpoint of 50 because the citable basis is now concentrated on the unreachable side of the split and the reachable side is judgment, not evidence.

evidence.claim: Chinese firms hold nine of the top ten global polysilicon manufacturer positions, led by Tongwei, GCL Technology, Daqo New Energy and Xinte Energy, who together held 65% of 2024 output; Wacker Chemie, the world's largest polysilicon producer from 2016 to 2019, had fallen to eighth place by 2024, the only non-Chinese firm in the top ten.
evidence.source_name: PV Tech, Chinese firms account for nine of the top ten polysilicon producers
source_excerpt: Chinese manufacturers account for nine of the world's top ten polysilicon producers, led by Tongwei, GCL Technology, Daqo New Energy and Xinte Energy.
the top four manufacturers accounting for 65% of the market share in 2024.
the world's largest polysilicon manufacturer between 2016 and 2019, but fell to fifth place in 2022 and then to eighth in 2024.

capture_odds.rationale: Re-sourced 2026-08-30. Neither previously cited item survived re-verification (one returned HTTP 403 with no reachable archive copy, the other's text contained none of the REC Silicon, Hemlock, or Wacker claims it was cited for), so this leg was left NULL and is now scored from two newly fetched, quoted sources. Shanghai Metals Market's trade-press analysis, fetched and quoted this run, puts the new US minimum import price of $21/kg for polysilicon at 4.3 to 4.4 times the Chinese spot price it assessed as of 2026-08-06 ($4.76-4.88/kg), and names Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker's US operations as the direct beneficiaries of that floor. A government-mandated wedge that size, if it holds and is enforced, is a real and substantial captured margin for the two named domestic producers, not merely 'some specs.' Two things hold the score well below the top of the range. First, the same article documents a leak already built into the mechanism: an importer can certify a fixed-term contract signed before 2026-08-06 to bypass the floor through the 2026-12-04 effective date, and a separate onshoring program lets approved companies import production equipment and covered products up to a Commerce-linked volume without paying the Section 232 duty at all, so a real share of near-term volume can route around the price the floor is meant to set, and enforcement beyond that carries no public registry of barred entities to check against. Second, and more directly, Wacker Chemie's own half-yearly financial report, fetched and quoted this run, a primary source published 2026-07-30 covering the six months to 2026-06-30, shows the Polysilicon division's EBITDA still down 41.6% year on year to EUR 33.9 million (EUR 58.0 million a year earlier), and the company's own outlook language names 'the still unresolved American trade policies on imports of polysilicon and its derivatives' as a source of 'a high degree of uncertainty' for its full-year forecast. That is the most current and most authoritative financial evidence available on either named beneficiary, filed weeks before the proclamation was even signed, and it shows the division still under margin pressure with management itself unwilling to underwrite the tariff's benefit yet. Scored 45: a real, quantified, unusually large price-floor mechanism that plausibly creates captured margin once enforced from 2026-12-04, held down from the top of the range by a stated contract-exemption leak, an untested certification and enforcement regime, and the most current company financials showing the effect has not yet appeared.

evidence.claim: The new US Section 232 minimum import price of $21/kg for polysilicon is approximately 4.3 to 4.4 times the Chinese spot price, which SMM assessed as of August 6, 2026 at RMB 32.95/kg and RMB 32.15/kg for n-type recycled feedstock and n-type dense polysilicon respectively, equivalent to about $4.88/kg and $4.76/kg at an exchange rate of RMB 6.7483 per US dollar (76.7% and 77.3% below the $21/kg floor); Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker's US operations are named as the direct beneficiaries of that floor, though a fixed-term contract signed before August 6, 2026, or Commerce's onshoring equipment-import program, can bypass it.
evidence.source_name: Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), US Finalizes Section 232 Measures on Polysilicon: Price Floors Could Reshape the U.S Solar Supply Chain
source_excerpt: As of August 6, SMM assessed average prices for n-type recycled feedstock and n-type dense polysilicon in China at RMB 32.95/kg and RMB 32.15/kg, respectively. Both had fallen by approximately 12.7% and 13.1% from April 1. Using an exchange rate of RMB 6.7483 per US dollar, the two prices were equivalent to approximately $4.88/kg and $4.76/kg. They were 76.7% and 77.3% below the US polysilicon MIP of $21/kg. Put differently, the US price floor is approximately 4.3-4.4 times the current Chinese spot price for n-type polysilicon.
For domestic polysilicon producers such as Hemlock Semiconductor and Wacker's US operations, the $21/kg MIP offers more direct price protection.
They may also document that the transaction is being executed under a fixed-term contract with fixed terms signed before August 6, 2026.

During construction, approved companies may import necessary production equipment and covered products at a volume linked by Commerce to the scale of the new investment without paying the applicable Section 232 duties.

evidence.claim: Wacker Chemie's Polysilicon division reported total sales of EUR 451.6 million in the first half of 2026, with EBITDA down 41.6% year on year to EUR 33.9 million from EUR 58.0 million a year earlier, and the company's own outlook states that the still-unresolved American trade policies on imports of polysilicon and its derivatives leave its full-year forecast subject to a high degree of uncertainty.
evidence.source_name: Wacker Chemie AG, Half-Yearly Financial Report, January 1 through June 30, 2026
source_excerpt: Polysilicon generated total sales of €451.6 million in the first half of 2026, down 3 percent year over year (€463.5 million). This drop was prompted mainly by lower prices in the solar-grade polysilicon business. By contrast, the semiconductor-grade polysilicon business once again performed very well, with volumes continuing to increase. The Polysilicon division's EBITDA in the reporting period amounted to €33.9 million, down by 41.6 percent on the figure of €58.0 million reported a year earlier.

Due to the currently unpredictable future developments in the Middle East and the still unresolved American trade policies on imports of polysilicon and its derivatives, the forecast is still subject to a high degree of uncertainty.

timing_fit.rationale: Re-verification pass, 2026-08-30: one of the two originally cited items did not fully hold up. The EY tax alert, cited for both the 2026-08-06 signing date and a Commerce Department investigation opened 2025-07-01, supports the signing date verbatim ('On 6 August 2026, the US President issued a proclamation...') but the investigation-opening date appears nowhere in the source; the page is also dated 2026-08-07, not 2026-08-10 as originally cited. Rather than soften the claim to keep only its supported half, the item is deleted; the signing date does not need re-citing here in any case, since it is the occurrence's own anchor_date. What survives is the Wiley alert, fetched and quoted this run, which independently carries both halves of the timing argument: the regime takes effect 'on or after 12:01 a.m. ET on December 4, 2026,' and the grandfathering clause names contracts 'entered into before August 6, 2026' as the exempt class. That is a signed, dated, mechanical trigger comfortably inside the 2 to 5 year window measured from the 2026-08-06 anchor. Held near the top of the range rather than at it, marked down slightly only because how strictly CBP applies the certification and ban provisions once the regime is live in December remains to be observed, and because this leg now rests on one citation rather than two.

evidence.claim: The tariff and minimum-import-price structure takes effect for goods entered for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. Eastern Time on December 4, 2026; importers must certify a compliant US sale price or that the goods are covered by a fixed-term contract entered into before August 6, 2026.
evidence.source_name: Wiley, Trump Administration Imposes Section 232 Tariffs and Minimum Import Prices on Polysilicon and its Derivatives
source_excerpt: The measures will take effect for goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. ET on December 4, 2026

Importers must provide documentation demonstrating that the first arm's-length sale of the imported merchandise (or downstream articles made from those imports) in the United States will occur at or above the applicable minimum import price or that the merchandise is being imported pursuant to fixed terms in a contract entered into before August 6, 2026.

notes.text: The finding here is not the headline money, it is where the floor's protection actually lands. The named commodity, polysilicon, is majority produced by Chinese firms this appraisal treats as unreachable, and the citable case for a listed US polysilicon winner does not currently exist in this file (the REC Silicon and Hemlock claims that would have made that case did not survive re-verification). If a chain is built here, it should start from the downstream cell and module assemblers and the utility developers whose 2026 build-out economics move, not from an assumption that a polysilicon price floor mechanically creates a listed polysilicon winner.
